question: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teammates disagreed on whether to refactor or patch a legacy module. I asked each to state their top concern in one sentence, then had the group vote on the risk we cared most about reducing first. We picked the patch path because the refactor risked a release date. The refactor was scheduled for the next quarter.
What did you do when one person kept interrupting?
I said 'let's capture that point on the board so we don't lose it' and moved to the next speaker.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: new grad on 4-person team fixing billing bug
Asked each person for one-sentence concern, then group vote on primary risk
Outcome: chose patch, deferred refactor to next quarter
Quote: 'let's capture that point on the board so we don't lose it'
Follow-up: handled interrupter by parking the point and moving on
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. Competency is Communication. The candidate described keeping a small-team disagreement on refactor vs patch moving by asking for one-sentence concerns and using a vote on risk. Quote: 'let's capture that point on the board so we don't lose it.' This shows basic ownership of keeping the discussion productive and learning to redirect interruptions. The outcome stayed within their individual scope. Biggest gap is lack of any follow-up metric on whether the patch actually worked.

lowerTranscript.text: Two people on my project disagreed about the design. I told them both their ideas were good and we should just try both. We ended up doing the one the senior engineer wanted.
How did you make sure both sides felt heard?
I just let them talk until they ran out of steam.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: new grad on small feature team
Told both sides their ideas were good and suggested trying both
Outcome: defaulted to senior engineer's preference
Quote: 'I just let them talk until they ran out of steam'
Follow-up: no structure or attempt to synthesize views
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Competency is Communication. The candidate defaulted to letting people talk until they stopped and then followed the senior person's preference. Quote: 'I just let them talk until they ran out of steam.' No evidence of owning the facilitation or learning how to surface trade-offs. The story shows passivity rather than any attempt to drive a clear outcome even at individual scope.

raiseTranscript.text: Platform and product teams disagreed on whether to prioritize API stability or new feature velocity. I ran a 90-minute session with data on past incidents and customer requests, then had each side list the top three risks of the other's approach. We landed on a phased rollout with a compatibility layer.
Support tickets on the new endpoints dropped 40% compared to the prior launch.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: senior on platform team influencing product
Used incident data and customer requests to frame session
Each side listed top three risks of the other approach
Outcome: phased rollout with compatibility layer
Quote: 'Support tickets on the new endpoints dropped 40% compared to the prior launch'
Follow-up: tracked and shared a concrete metric
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Competency is Communication. The candidate used data on incidents and requests to structure a cross-team debate on API stability vs velocity, then had each side articulate the other's risks. Quote on the 40% drop in support tickets shows measurable cross-team impact. Influence happened without authority. Biggest strength is the clear before-and-after metric attached to the decision.

lowerTranscript.text: The two teams kept pushing their own roadmaps. I summarized both positions in an email and asked the directors to decide. The email got forwarded around but nothing changed for two months.
Did you try any live facilitation?
I offered to schedule a meeting but both sides said they were too busy.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: senior trying to align platform and product
Sent summary email and deferred to directors
Outcome: two-month stall with no decision
Quote: 'both sides said they were too busy'
Follow-up: no attempt to run the meeting or surface trade-offs directly
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. Competency is Communication. The candidate sent an email summary and waited for directors to decide, resulting in a two-month stall. Quote: 'both sides said they were too busy.' No evidence of using influence without authority or creating a structured discussion. The story shows escalation rather than facilitation and lacks any cross-team outcome.

raiseTranscript.text: My team split on whether to adopt a new review process that added mandatory design docs. I had the two strongest opponents each run a two-week pilot on one of their projects and present results to the team. The data showed fewer late-stage changes, so we adopted a lighter version.
How did you handle the person who still disagreed after the pilot?
I asked them to own the next retro on whether the lighter version was working and report back.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: manager of 8-person team debating review process
Opponents ran pilots and presented data to the team
Outcome: adopted lighter version of the process
Quote: 'I asked them to own the next retro on whether the lighter version was working'
Follow-up: gave dissenting voice ownership of follow-up measurement
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Competency is Communication. The candidate turned a team split on mandatory design docs into a data-driven pilot run by the opponents themselves. Quote about asking the remaining dissenter to own the next retro shows developing people and creating team leverage. Outcome improved the process while addressing underperformance in collaboration. Biggest strength is converting conflict into ownership.

lowerTranscript.text: Half the team wanted the new process, half didn't. I made the call to go with the majority and announced it in the next team meeting. A couple people were quiet afterward.
How did you check whether the decision landed well?
I asked in the next 1:1s but didn't bring it up in a group setting again.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: manager of team split on process change
Decided by majority vote and announced in meeting
Outcome: some team members stayed quiet
Quote: 'I asked in the next 1:1s but didn't bring it up in a group setting again'
Follow-up: avoided group follow-up on the decision
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. Competency is Communication. The candidate used majority vote and announced the decision without further group discussion. Quote: 'I asked in the next 1:1s but didn't bring it up in a group setting again.' No evidence of developing the team or handling underperformance in collaboration. The story shows top-down resolution rather than creating leverage through the team.

raiseTranscript.text: Engineering and sales leadership disagreed on whether to invest in a new enterprise feature that would delay the SMB roadmap by two quarters. I ran a series of sessions using win-rate data and churn analysis, then asked each side to model the three-year revenue impact of both paths. We chose the enterprise bet but ring-fenced 20% of engineering time for SMB work.
Enterprise revenue grew 3x in 18 months while SMB churn stayed flat.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: VP engineering aligning with sales on roadmap trade-off
Used win-rate and churn data plus three-year modeling
Outcome: enterprise investment with 20% time ring-fenced for SMB
Quote: 'Enterprise revenue grew 3x in 18 months while SMB churn stayed flat'
Follow-up: tracked multi-quarter business outcome
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Competency is Communication. The candidate structured multi-session debate between engineering and sales using revenue modeling and protected a portion of capacity for the other segment. Quote on 3x enterprise growth with flat SMB churn shows org-level impact and strategic trade-off handling. The approach created long-term leverage rather than a one-time win. Biggest strength is the explicit long-term metric tied to the decision.

lowerTranscript.text: Sales wanted the enterprise feature; engineering wanted to stay on the current plan. I listened to both sides in separate meetings and then told the teams we would split the difference by adding the feature in the following quarter.
How did you align the two organizations on the timeline?
I sent a note to the leadership team and moved on to the next planning cycle.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of facilitating a discussion where people held strongly opposing views.
Role: VP trying to resolve sales vs engineering roadmap conflict
Met separately then announced a compromise timeline
Outcome: no joint modeling or shared ownership
Quote: 'I sent a note to the leadership team and moved on to the next planning cycle'
Follow-up: avoided ongoing alignment work
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. Competency is Communication. The candidate met separately with each side and announced a compromise via note. Quote: 'I sent a note to the leadership team and moved on to the next planning cycle.' No evidence of strategic judgment or long-term trade-off modeling at the org level. The story shows avoidance of ambiguity rather than creating shared understanding.

diagnostic.exec: Models multi-year revenue impact and protects capacity for both paths
